source_text: Καὶ τί λέγω πᾶσιν; οὐδὲ γὰρ αὐτοῖς τοῖς ἀποστόλοις καὶ τοῖς μαθηταῖς ἀεὶ συνῆν ἢ ἀεὶ ἐφαίνετο. μὴ δυναμένοις αὐτοῦ χωρῆσαι τὴν θεωρίαν διηνεκῶς. λαμπροτέρα γὰρ τὴν οἰκονομίαν τελέσαντος ἡ θειότης ἦν αὐτοῦ, ἥντινα Κηφᾶς ὁ Πέτρος ὡσπερεὶ „ἀπαρχὴ“ τῶν ἀποστόλων δεδύνηται ἰδεῖν, καὶ μετ᾿ αὐτὸν οἱ δώδεκα, τοῦ Ματθίου ἀντὶ τοῦ Ἰούδα καταταχθέντος, καὶ μετ᾿ ἐκείνους „πεντακοσίοις ἀδελφοῖς ἐφάπαξ.“ „ἔπειτα ὤφθη Ἰακώβῳ. ἔπειτα τοῖς“ ἑτέροις παρὰ τοὺς δώδεκα „ἀποστόλοις πᾶσι.“ τάχα τοῖς ἑβδομήκοντα. „ἔσχατον δὲ πάντων“ Παύλῳ τῷ ὡσπερεὶ „ἐκτρώματι“ καὶ ἐπισταμένῳ. πῶς ἔλεγεν· „ἐμοὶ τῷ ἐλαχιστοτέρῳ πάντων ἁγίων ἐδόθη ἡ χάρις αὕτη.“ καὶ τάχα τὸ „ἐλαχιστοτέρῳ“ ἴσον ἐστὶ τῷ „ἐκτρώματι.“ ὥσπερ οὖν οὐκ ἄν τις εὐκόλως ἐγκαλέσαι τῷ Ἰησοῦ μὴ παραλαμβάνοντι πάντας τοὺς ἀποστόλους εἰς τὸ ὑψηλὸν ὄρος ἀλλὰ μόνους τοὺς προειρημένους τρεῖς. ἡνίκα ἔμελλε μεταμορφοῦσθαι καὶ τὴν λαμπρότητα δεικνύναι τῶν ἱματίων ἑαυτοῦ καὶ τὴν δόξαν Μωϋσέως καὶ Ἠλίου συλλαλούντων αὐτῷ. οὕτως οὖν οὐκ ἂν τοῖς ἀποστολικοῖς λόγοις μέμφοιτ᾿ ἄν τις εὐλόγως εἰσάγουσιν ὦφθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν μετὰ τὴν ἀνάστασιν οὐ πᾶσιν. ἀλλ᾿ οἷς εἶδεν ἀνειληφόσιν ὀφθαλμοὺς χωροῦντας ἰδεῖν τὴν ἀνάστασιν αὐτοῦ. χρήσιμον δ᾿ οἶμαι πρὸς ἀπολογίαν τῶν προκειμένων ἐστὶ καὶ τὸ οὕτως εἰρημένον περὶ αὐτοῦ· „εἰς τοῦτο γὰρ Χριστὸς ἀπέθανε καὶ ἀνέστη. ἵνα καὶ νεκρῶν καὶ ζώντων κυριεύσῃ.“ ὅρα γὰρ ἐν τούτοις ὅτι „ἀπέθανεν“ Ἰησοῦς. „ἵνα νεκρῶν κυριεύσῃ.“ „καὶ ἀνέστη, ἵνα“ μὴ μόνον „νεκρῶν“ ἀλλὰ „καὶ ζώντων κυριεύσῃ.“ καὶ οἶδέ γε ὁ ἀπόστολος νεκροὺς μὲν. ὧν κυριεύει ὁ Χριστὸς. τοὺς οὕτως κατειλεγμένους ἐν τῇ πρὸς Κορινθίους προτέρᾳ· „σαλπίσει γὰρ. καὶ οἱ νεκροὶ ἐγερθήσονται ἄφθαρτοι.“ ζῶντας δὲ αὐτοὺς καὶ τοὺς ἀλλαγησομένους. ἑτέρους ὄντας τῶν ἐγερθησομένων νεκρῶν, ἔχει δὲ καὶ περὶ τούτων ἡ λέξις οὕτως· „καὶ ἡμεῖς ἀλλαγησόμεθα.“ ἑξῆς εἰρημένη τῷ „οἱ νεκροὶ ἐγερθήσονται πρῶτον.“ ἀλλὰ καὶ ἐν τῇ πρὸς Θεσσαλονικεῖς προτέρᾳ ἐν ἑτέραις λέξεσι τὴν αὐτὴν διαφορὰν παριστὰς. φησὶν ἄλλους μὲν εἶναι τοὺς κοιμωμένους ἄλλους δὲ τοὺς ζῶντας λέγων· „οὐ θέλομεν δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀγνοεῖν, ἀδελφοὶ, περὶ τῶν κοιμωμένων, ἵνα μὴ λυπῆσθε ὡς καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ οἱ μὴ ἔχοντες ἐλπίδα. εἰ γὰρ πιστεύομεν ὅτι Ἰησοῦς ἀπέθανε καὶ ἀνέστη, οὕτως καὶ ὁ θεὸς τοὺς κοιμηθέντας διὰ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ ἄξει σὺν αὐτῷ. τοῦτο γὰρ ὑμῖν λέγομεν ἐν λόγῳ κυρίου, ὅτι ἡμεῖς οἱ ζῶντες οἱ περιλειπόμενοι εἰς τὴν παρουσίαν τοῦ κυρίου οὐ μὴ φθάσωμεν τοὺς κοιμηθέντας.“ τὴν δὲ φανεῖσαν ἡμῖν εἰς τοὺς τόπους διήγησιν ἐξεθέμεθα ἐν οἷς ὑπηγορεύσαμεν ἐξηγητικοῖς τῆς πρὸς Θεσσαλονικεῖς προτέρας ἐπιστολῆς.
pass_a_gloss: And why do I say (λέγω) 'to all' (πᾶσιν)? For not even (οὐδέ) with the apostles themselves and the disciples (μαθηταί) was he always (ἀεί) present (συνῆν) or always appearing (ἐφαίνετο), they not being able (μὴ δυναμένοις) to contain/take in (χωρῆσαι) the sight/contemplation (θεωρία) of him continuously (διηνεκῶς). For more radiant (λαμπροτέρα) was his divinity (θειότης) when he had completed (τελέσαντος) the economy/dispensation (οἰκονομία), which Cephas the Peter, as it were 'firstfruits' (ἀπαρχή) of the apostles, has been able (δεδύνηται) to see, and after him the twelve, Matthias having been ranked/appointed (καταταχθέντος) in place of Judas, and after those 'to five hundred brothers at once (ἐφάπαξ).' 'Then he was seen (ὤφθη) by James, then by' the other, besides the twelve, 'all the apostles,' perhaps (τάχα) the seventy; 'and last of all (ἔσχατον πάντων)' by Paul, as it were 'the miscarriage/untimely birth (ἔκτρωμα),' and knowing (ἐπισταμένῳ) how he was saying: 'to me, the leaster (ἐλαχιστότερος, comparative of superlative) of all saints, this grace (χάρις) was given.' And perhaps 'leaster' is equal (ἴσον) to 'miscarriage.' So just as one would not easily (εὐκόλως) accuse (ἐγκαλέσαι) Jesus for not taking along (παραλαμβάνοντι) all the apostles to the high mountain but only the three mentioned before, when he was about to be transformed (μεταμορφοῦσθαι) and to show the brightness (λαμπρότης) of his garments and the glory (δόξα) of Moses and Elijah talking with (συλλαλούντων) him, so one would not reasonably (εὐλόγως) blame (μέμφοιτο) the apostolic words (ἀποστολικοὶ λόγοι) for introducing (εἰσάγουσιν) that Jesus had been seen after the resurrection not by all, but by those whom he saw having taken up (ἀνειληφόσιν) eyes able to contain (χωροῦντας) seeing his resurrection. Useful (χρήσιμον), I think, for the defence (ἀπολογία) of the matters lying before (προκείμενα) is also what is thus said about him: 'For to this (εἰς τοῦτο) Christ died and rose, that he might be lord (κυριεύσῃ) of both dead and living.' See in these that Jesus 'died' 'that he might lord it over the dead,' 'and rose, that' not only 'of the dead' but 'also of the living he might be lord.' And the apostle knows as dead, of whom Christ is lord, those thus listed (κατειλεγμένους) in the first to the Corinthians: 'for it will trumpet (σαλπίσει), and the dead will be raised (ἐγερθήσονται) incorruptible (ἄφθαρτοι)'; and as living, those who will be changed (ἀλλαγησομένους), being other than the dead who will be raised; and the wording (λέξις) about these too runs thus: 'and we shall be changed,' said next after 'the dead will be raised first.' But also in the first to the Thessalonians, presenting (παριστάς) in other words (λέξεσι) the same difference (διαφορά), he says that some are the sleeping (κοιμώμενοι) and others the living, saying: 'We do not wish you to be ignorant (ἀγνοεῖν), brothers, about the sleeping, that you may not grieve (λυπῆσθε) as also the rest who do not have hope (ἐλπίς). For if we believe that Jesus died and rose, so also God will bring (ἄξει) with him those who fell asleep through Jesus. For this we say to you in a word of the Lord (ἐν λόγῳ κυρίου), that we the living, those remaining (περιλειπόμενοι) to the coming (παρουσία) of the Lord, shall by no means precede (οὐ μὴ φθάσωμεν) those who fell asleep.' The account/exposition (διήγησις) of the places (τόποι) that appeared [right] to us we set out in the exegetical [writings] we dictated (ὑπηγορεύσαμεν) on the first epistle to the Thessalonians.
pass_b_english: And why do I say “to all”? For not even with the apostles and disciples themselves was he always present, or always visible to them, since they could not take in the sight of him without a break. For once he had completed the dispensation, his divinity shone more brightly. Cephas, that is Peter, as it were the “firstfruits” of the apostles, was able to see it; after him the Twelve, Matthias having been appointed in place of Judas (Acts 1:26); and after them “five hundred brothers at one time.” “Then he appeared to James, then to all the” other “apostles” besides the Twelve, perhaps to the Seventy (Luke 10:1); “and last of all” to Paul, as to “one untimely born” (1 Corinthians 15:5–8). Paul knew well in what sense he said, “To me, less than the least of all the saints, this grace was given” (Ephesians 3:8); and perhaps “less than the least” means the same as “untimely born.”

Just as, then, no one could readily find fault with Jesus for not taking all the apostles up the high mountain, but only the three already named, when he was about to be transfigured and to show the brightness of his garments and the glory of Moses and Elijah talking with him (Matthew 17:1–3), so no one could reasonably blame the apostles’ accounts for relating that after the resurrection Jesus was seen not by all, but by those whom he saw had gained eyes able to see his resurrection.

I think these words said about him also help the defence of what is before us: “For to this end Christ died and rose, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living” (Romans 14:9). Notice in these words that Jesus “died” “that he might be Lord of the dead,” “and rose, that he might be Lord” not only “of the dead” but “also of the living.” And the apostle does know as the dead over whom Christ is Lord those he lists in this way in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “For the trumpet will sound, and the dead will be raised imperishable” (1 Corinthians 15:52); and as the living, those who will be changed, who are other than the dead who will be raised. About these too the passage reads: “and we shall be changed” (1 Corinthians 15:52), said right after “the dead will be raised first” (compare 1 Thessalonians 4:16).

In the First Epistle to the Thessalonians as well he sets out the same distinction in other words, and says that those who sleep are one group and the living another: “We do not want you to be ignorant, brothers, about those who are asleep, so that you may not grieve as the rest do who have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so God will bring with him those who have fallen asleep through Jesus. For this we tell you by the word of the Lord, that we who are alive, who are left until the coming of the Lord, will by no means go before those who have fallen asleep” (1 Thessalonians 4:13–15). The interpretation of these passages that seemed right to us we have set out in the commentaries we dictated on the First Epistle to the Thessalonians.

choices.why: Restored 'For' (γάρ) at 'For not even with the apostles'.
χωρῆσαι: 'bear the sight' -> 'take in the sight' (capacity, not endurance; matches 2.66-67).
ἐπισταμένῳ πῶς ἔλεγεν: 'understood what he meant' -> 'knew well in what sense he said'.
Restored emphatic γε: 'And the apostle does know'.

translator_notes: Opening ‘why do I say “to all”’ takes up Celsus’s demand (2.63) that Jesus should have appeared ‘to all’; marked as a quoted phrase. ‘ἀπαρχή’ (firstfruits) for Peter is set in quotation marks by the edition; it is Origen’s use of a Pauline word (compare 1 Corinthians 15:20, 23, where Christ is the firstfruits), not a quotation about Peter, so no citation is placed on it. The list follows 1 Corinthians 15:5-8; Origen’s glosses (‘the other apostles besides the Twelve’, ‘perhaps the Seventy’) are kept outside the quotation marks as in the edition; the Seventy cited to Luke 10:1. Matthias: Acts 1:26. ‘ἐλαχιστότερος’ is a comparative built on a superlative; rendered ‘less than the least’ to keep Origen’s point that it matches ‘untimely born’. ‘ἐπισταμένῳ πῶς ἔλεγεν’ rendered ‘understood what he meant when he said’. Romans 14:9: Origen reads ‘ἀπέθανε καὶ ἀνέστη’ (died and rose); the received NT text has ‘ἀπέθανεν καὶ ἔζησεν’ (died and lived); rendered as Origen quotes. ‘σαλπίσει’ (impersonal ‘it will trumpet’) rendered ‘the trumpet will sound’. The phrase ‘the dead will be raised first’ combines 1 Corinthians 15:52 with 1 Thessalonians 4:16 (‘the dead in Christ will rise first’); cited with ‘compare’. Transfiguration cited to Matthew 17:1-3 (compare Mark 9:2-4; Luke 9:28-31). The commentary on 1 Thessalonians mentioned at the end is lost. Stray full stops in the edition’s punctuation (e.g. ‘Ἰακώβῳ. ἔπειτα’) read through.
